concept.name: Exchange-traded fund
concept.definition: An exchange-traded investment product that must register with the SEC as an open-end investment company (or sometimes as a unit investment trust). It pools investor money into a portfolio of assets and its shares trade on a national securities exchange throughout the day at market prices, like a stock.
concept.intuition: An ETF packages a whole portfolio into a single share you can buy or sell any time the market is open, combining mutual-fund-style pooling with stock-style trading.
concept.mechanics: Large broker-dealers called authorized participants create and redeem ETF shares in large blocks (creation units, typically 50,000 shares or more), usually in exchange for baskets of the underlying securities in-kind. This creation/redemption arbitrage keeps the ETF's market price close to its net asset value.
concept.failure_modes: In stressed markets the ETF's price can trade at a premium or discount to NAV, and the liquidity of the underlying assets may be much thinner than the ETF's own trading liquidity suggests. Tracking error, fees, and, for leveraged or inverse ETFs, daily-reset compounding can produce returns far from the index multiple investors expect.
concept.misconceptions: That all ETFs are cheap, passive index trackers — the wrapper also wraps leveraged, inverse, actively managed, and single-commodity products with very different risks. Also, ETF shares are not redeemed for cash by ordinary investors; they are sold on the exchange.
concept.example: An investor buys 100 shares of an S&P 500 ETF on an exchange at 10:30 a.m. at the prevailing market price, gaining diversified index exposure in one intraday trade.
